newsitem.title: ALBANIA: OSCE endorses Albanian general election.
newsitem.headline: OSCE endorses Albanian general election.

text.p: The pan-European body overseeing Albania's general election endorsed the vote on Monday as "adequate and acceptable" and said it was a foundation for a stable democracy after months of turmoil.

A preliminary statement read by Catherine Lalumiere, the top official observing the election for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, said the vote had showed Albanians' desire for a democratic future "despite minor flaws in many areas and some very serious problems in a few areas".
"We believe therefore that we can say that the elections can be considered as adequate and acceptable," the statement said.
"The result of these elections can be the foundation for a stable, democratic system, which Albanians want and deserve."
A full report will be issued later after the completion next week of run-off elections in districts where no candidate won 50 percent of the vote.
The preliminary report said the elections had been characterised by a large turnout, relatively few incidents of intimidation, and non-partisan conduct from most electoral commissions.
In the most serious election incident, a returning officer in a village near the southern town of Fier was shot and killed during Sunday's poll.

Several instances of ballot papers or boxes being stolen or tampered with were also recorded, but there was none of the wholesale violence which has gripped the country for months and killed at least 1,500 people.
The OSCE had sent more than 450 observers all over the rugged country to help ensure a free vote 13 months after the last general elections were found to have been unfair.

Top OSCE officials, including the head of the mission, former Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, had admitted before the election that the vote was unlikely to meet fully all Western criteria for fair elections.

Official results of Sunday's vote have been slow in coming in but President Sali Berisha has admitted the defeat of his Democratic Party. The opposition Socialists say that along with allied parties they should have a two-thirds majority in the 155-seat assembly.
